radii.title: One Earth radius, measured {{all}} ways, in two honest groups
radii.mini: Pressure waves timed round the planet, satellite Doppler, airliner flight times and a medieval hill-and-horizon measurement: {{k}} methods whose data the radius never entered give {{mean}} ± {{se}} km. {{ck}} more, whose data once touched a globe model, are kept apart: {{cmean}} ± {{cse}} km.
radii.text: Each line is one method run backwards, so that real data give the Earth's radius. They come in two groups that are never mixed. Measurements, where the radius never entered the data: the Hunga Tonga pressure wave timed both ways round on barometers [12], the same kind of wave from Krakatoa in 1883, one lap at a time on the Royal Society's barographs [13], airliner flight times against the angle between airports and the filed airspeed [6], the distances of the receivers from the centre the satellites orbit, from one day of satellite Doppler with every orbit and receiver free [14], and al-Bīrūnī's hill-and-horizon measurement of about 1018, quoted, not recomputed [9]. Weighted by the inverse of their variances, {{n}} of the {{k}} give R = {{mean}} ± {{se}} km, {{z}} standard errors from the mean radius of 6,371 km (dashed line); χ² = {{chi2}} for {{dof}} degrees of freedom, Birge ratio {{birge}} [11]. Checks, where a distance computed on the globe, a reference model or a speed measured with globe distances entered the data at some point: seismic surface waves [1], reciprocal zenith angles between survey stations [2][3], stars setting behind a mountain crest [4], an aircraft's weight flying east and west [5], and the author's photograph of the sea horizon and filmed sunset [7][8]. They give {{cmean}} ± {{cse}} km ({{cn}} of {{ck}} counted; shown but not counted: {{nc}}). Box: the middle half of a method's values; thick tick: its median; thin line: its full range; black bar: its total uncertainty, statistical plus a systematic part measured by redoing it with the other reductions it allows, such as another refraction coefficient [10]. None was tuned to land near 6,371 km. On a plane, the surveying, theodolite and dip methods return an infinite radius, and the others find no distances that fit.
radii.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the measurements whose data the radius never entered returning an infinite radius or no radius at all, or disagreeing with one another far beyond their uncertainties.
motion.title: The Earth's spin and the size of its orbit, measured several ways
motion.mini: Ring lasers, falling balls and satellite Doppler give the Earth's rotation; aberration and light time the size of its orbit, checked by Doppler shifts, the transits of Venus, Venus radar and pulsars. All cluster at the accepted values, far from a flat model's.
motion.text: Each line is one method; dots are its individual values and the tick their median. Top: the rotation Ω, from two horizontal ring lasers whose beat frequency is the rotation they feel [1], from balls falling east of the plumb line [2], and from one day of satellite Doppler fitted with every orbit and every receiver free [3]. Bottom: the Earth–Sun distance, from Bradley's aberration and Delambre's light time [4], and, as checks, from the Doppler shifts of the Sun and of τ Ceti [5], the transits of Venus of 1761, 1769 and 2012 [6], radar echoes from Venus in 1961 [7] and the yearly delay of twelve pulsars [8]. Blue: measurements whose data the quantity never entered; violet: checks. The dashed lines are the accepted values, for comparison only. Both axes start at zero, where the flat models put their answers: a plane at rest does not turn, and the flat model's Sun is a few thousand kilometres up. The falling balls scatter widely, and the figure shows it.
motion.verdict: Would favour the flat model: methods measuring no rotation at all, or an Earth–Sun distance of a few thousand kilometres.
